verses.32:11: For I waited for your words; I listened to your prudence while you were debating with words,
verses.32:12: and as long as I thought you were saying something, I paid careful attention; but, as I see, there is no one among you who can refute Job and answer his words.
verses.32:13: Beware that you do not say, 'We have found wisdom; God has thrown him down, not man.'
verses.32:14: He spoke nothing to me, and for my part I will not answer him according to your words.
verses.32:15: They became afraid and answered no longer, and they removed speech from themselves.
verses.32:16: Since, therefore, I waited and they did not speak—they stood still and did not answer any further—
verses.32:17: I too will answer my part, and I will show my knowledge.
verses.32:18: For I am full of words, and the spirit within my belly constrains me.
verses.32:19: Look, my belly is like new wine without a vent, which bursts new flasks.
verses.32:20: I will speak and catch my breath a little; I will open my lips and answer.
verses.32:21: I will not show partiality toward a man, and I will not equate God with a human being.
verses.32:22: For I do not know how long I will endure, and whether after a little while my Maker may take me away."
verses.33:1: "Hear, therefore, Job, my utterances, and listen closely to all my words.
verses.33:2: Look, I have opened my mouth; let my tongue speak in my throat.
verses.33:3: My words are from my sincere heart, and my lips will speak a pure conviction.
verses.33:4: The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty has given life to me.
verses.33:5: If you are able, answer me, and take your stand before my face.
verses.33:6: Look, God made me just as He made you, and from the same clay I too was formed.
verses.33:7: Nevertheless, do not let my wonder terrify you, nor let my eloquence be heavy upon you.
verses.33:8: You said, therefore, in my ears, and I heard the sound of your words:
verses.33:9: 'I am clean and without offense, unblemished, and there is no iniquity in me.
verses.33:10: Because He has found complaints against me, therefore He has regarded me as an enemy to Himself.
verses.33:11: He has placed my feet in the stocks; He has watched all my paths.'
verses.33:12: This, therefore, is the point in which you are not justified: I will answer you, for God is greater than man.
verses.33:13: Do you contend against Him because He has not answered you concerning all words?
verses.33:14: God speaks once, and He does not repeat the same thing a second time.
verses.33:15: Through a dream, in a night vision, when deep sleep comes upon men and they sleep on a bed,
verses.33:16: then He opens the ears of men, and teaching them, He instructs them with discipline,
verses.33:17: so that He may turn a man away from the things he does, and deliver him from pride,
verses.33:18: rescuing his soul from corruption, and his life, so that it may not pass over to the sword.
verses.33:19: He also rebukes him through pain on a bed, and causes all his bones to wither.
verses.33:20: Bread becomes detestable to him in his life, and to his soul the food that was formerly desirable.
verses.33:21: His flesh will waste away, and the bones that had been covered will be laid bare.
verses.33:22: His soul has drawn close to corruption, and his life to those who bring death.
verses.33:23: If there is an angel speaking on his behalf, one out of thousands, to declare a man's uprightness,
verses.33:24: he will show mercy to him and say, 'Deliver him, so that he does not descend into corruption; I have found that by which I may be gracious to him.'
verses.33:25: His flesh has been consumed by torments; let him return to the days of his youth.
verses.33:26: He will plead with God, and He will be favorable to him; and he will see His face with rejoicing, and He will restore to the man his righteousness.
verses.33:27: He will look upon men and say, 'I have sinned and truly committed an offense, and I did not receive as I deserved.'
verses.33:28: He has delivered his soul, so that it might not go into destruction, but living might see the light.
verses.33:29: Look, God works all these things three times with each individual,
verses.33:30: so that He may call back their souls from corruption, and illuminate them with the light of the living.
verses.33:31: Pay attention, Job, and listen to me; and be silent while I speak.
verses.33:32: But if you have something to say, answer me; speak, for I want you to appear righteous.
verses.33:33: But if you do not, listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you wisdom."
verses.34:1: And so Elihu, speaking out, also said these things:
verses.34:2: "Hear my words, you who are wise, and listen to me, you who are learned.
verses.34:3: For the ear tests words, and the throat discerns foods by taste.
verses.34:4: Let us choose judgment for ourselves, and among ourselves let us see what is better.
verses.34:5: For Job has said, 'I am righteous, and God has subverted my justice.
verses.34:6: For there is falsehood in judging me; my arrow is violent without any sin.'
verses.34:7: What man is like Job, who drinks derision like water,
verses.34:8: who goes with those who work iniquity and walks with wicked men?
verses.34:9: For he has said, 'A man will not please God, even if he runs with Him.'
verses.34:10: Therefore, prudent men, hear me: may wickedness be far from God, and iniquity from the Almighty.
verses.34:11: For He will repay a man's work to him, and according to the ways of each one He will recompense them.
verses.34:12: For truly God will not condemn without cause, nor will the Almighty subvert justice.
verses.34:13: Whom else has He appointed over the earth? Or whom has He placed over the world that He fashioned?
verses.34:14: If He directs His heart toward him, He will draw his spirit and breath to Himself.
verses.34:15: All flesh will fail together, and man will return to ashes.
verses.34:16: Therefore, if you have understanding, hear what is said, and listen to the voice of my speech:
verses.34:17: Can one who does not love justice be healed? And how do you condemn Him who is righteous to such an extent?
verses.34:18: He who says to a king, 'Apostate,' who calls leaders wicked,
verses.34:19: who does not show partiality to princes, nor did He regard the tyrant when he contended against the poor man; for all of them are the work of His hands.
verses.34:20: Suddenly they will die, and in the middle of the night the peoples will be thrown into turmoil; and they will pass away, and they will remove the violent one without a hand.
verses.34:21: For His eyes are on the ways of men, and He observes all their steps.
verses.34:22: There is no darkness, and there is no shadow of death, where those who work iniquity can be hidden;
verses.34:23: for it is no longer in a man's power to come to God for judgment.
verses.34:24: He will crush many, and countless ones, and He will make others stand in their place.
verses.34:25: For He knows their works, and for that reason He will bring on night, and they will be crushed.
verses.34:26: As wicked men He struck them in the place of onlookers,
verses.34:27: who as if on purpose turned away from Him, and were unwilling to understand all His ways,
verses.34:28: so that they caused the cry of the needy one to come to Him, and He would hear the voice of the poor.
verses.34:29: For when He Himself grants peace, who is there who can condemn? From the moment He hides His face, who is there who can gaze upon Him, both over nations and over all men?
verses.34:30: He who makes a hypocritical man reign because of the sins of the people.
verses.34:31: Since therefore I have spoken to God, I will not restrain you either.
verses.34:32: If I have erred, you teach me; if I have spoken iniquity, I will add nothing further.
verses.34:33: Does God demand it from you because it displeased you? For you began to speak, and not I; now if you know anything better, speak.
verses.34:34: Let men with understanding speak to me, and let a wise man hear me.
verses.34:35: But Job has spoken foolishly, and his words do not ring with instruction.
verses.34:36: My Father, let Job be tested all the way to the end; do not leave off from the man of iniquity.
verses.34:37: Because he adds blasphemy on top of his sins, let him be bound among us in the meantime, and then let him challenge God to judgment with his statements."
verses.35:1: Therefore Elihu spoke these things again:
verses.35:2: "Does your thinking seem fair to you, that you should say, 'I am more righteous than God'?
verses.35:3: For you have said, 'What is upright does not please You; or what will it benefit You if I sin?'
verses.35:4: Therefore I will respond to your statements, and to your friends with you.
verses.35:5: Look up to heaven and gaze, and observe the upper sky, that it is higher than you.
verses.35:6: If you sin, how will you harm Him? And if your iniquities are multiplied, what will you do against Him?
verses.35:7: Moreover, if you act righteously, what will you give Him? Or what will He receive from your hand?
verses.35:8: Your wickedness will harm a man who is like you, and your righteousness will help a son of man.
verses.35:9: Because of the multitude of false accusers they will cry out, and they will wail because of the force of the arm of tyrants.
verses.35:10: And he has not said, 'Where is God who made me, who gave songs in the night,
verses.35:11: who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth, and instructs us more than the birds of heaven?'
verses.35:12: There they will cry out, and He will not answer, because of the pride of evil people.
verses.35:13: Therefore God will not hear in vain, and the Almighty will examine the cases of each one.
verses.35:14: Even when you say, 'He does not observe,' be judged before Him, and wait for Him.
verses.35:15: For now He does not inflict His fury, nor does He severely punish wrongdoing.
verses.35:16: Therefore Job opens his mouth in vain, and without knowledge he multiplies words."
verses.36:1: Elihu also continued and spoke these things:
verses.36:2: "Bear with me a little, and I will show you, for I still have something to speak on behalf of God.
verses.36:3: I will trace my knowledge from the beginning, and I will prove my Maker righteous.
verses.36:4: For truly my words are without falsehood, and perfect knowledge will be proved to you.
verses.36:5: God does not reject the mighty, since He Himself is also mighty;
verses.36:6: but He does not save the wicked, and He grants justice to the poor.
verses.36:7: He will not withdraw His eyes from the righteous, and He places kings on the throne forever, and they are lifted up.
verses.36:8: And if they are in chains and are bound with cords of poverty,
verses.36:9: He will show them their deeds and their crimes, because they were violent.
verses.36:10: He will also open their ear to correct them, and He will speak so that they may turn back from iniquity.
verses.36:11: If they listen and obey, they will complete their days in good and their years in glory;
verses.36:12: but if they do not listen, they will pass through the sword and be consumed in folly.
verses.36:13: Hypocrites and the crafty provoke the wrath of God, nor will they cry out when they are bound.
verses.36:14: Their soul will die in a storm, and their life among the effeminate.
verses.36:15: He will rescue the poor man from his distress, and He will open his ear in affliction.
verses.36:16: Therefore He will save you most broadly from a mouth that is narrow and has no foundation beneath it, and the rest of your table will be full of fatness.
verses.36:17: Your cause has been judged like that of a wicked man; you will receive cause and judgment.
verses.36:18: Therefore do not let wrath overpower you so that you oppress anyone, nor let a great number of gifts sway you.
verses.36:19: Lay down your greatness without affliction, and all the mighty in strength.
verses.36:20: Do not prolong the night, so that peoples may ascend in their place.
verses.36:21: Take care that you do not turn aside to iniquity, for you have begun to follow this after misery.
verses.36:22: Look, God is exalted in His strength, and no one is like Him among lawgivers.
verses.36:23: Who will be able to search out His ways? Or who can say to Him, 'You have done iniquity'?
verses.36:24: Remember that you do not know His work, about which men have sung.
verses.36:25: All people see Him; each one gazes from afar.
verses.36:26: Look, God is great, surpassing our knowledge; the number of His years is incalculable.
verses.36:27: He draws up the drops of rain and pours out showers like torrents,
verses.36:28: which flow from the clouds that cover all things from above.
verses.36:29: If He wills to spread out the clouds like His tent,
verses.36:30: and to flash with His light from above, He will also cover the hinges of the sea.
verses.36:31: For through these things He judges peoples and gives food to many mortals.
verses.36:32: In His hands He hides the light, and He has commanded it to come again.
verses.36:33: He announces concerning it to His friend, that it is his possession and that he can ascend to it."
verses.37:1: "At this my heart has shuddered and has been moved out of its place.
verses.37:2: Listen attentively in the terror of His voice, and to the sound proceeding from His mouth.
verses.37:3: Beneath all the heavens He Himself observes, and His light is over the ends of the earth.
verses.37:4: After Him a sound will roar; He will thunder with the voice of His greatness, and it will not be traced out when His voice is heard.
verses.37:5: God will thunder marvelously with His voice, He who does great and unsearchable things;
verses.37:6: who commands the snow to descend to the earth, and the winter rains, and the shower of His strength;
verses.37:7: who sets a seal in the hand of all people, so that each one may know his own works.
verses.37:8: The wild beast will enter a hiding place and will remain in its den.
verses.37:9: From the inner recesses the storm will come forth, and from Arcturus the cold.
verses.37:10: When God blows, frost congeals, and again very wide waters are poured out.
verses.37:11: Grain longs for clouds, and the clouds scatter their light.
verses.37:12: They move around in a circuit wherever the will of Him who governs leads them, for everything that He commands them over the face of the world:
verses.37:13: whether in one tribe, or in His land, or in whatever place of His mercy He commands them to be found.
verses.37:14: Listen to these things, Job; stand still and consider the marvels of God.
verses.37:15: Do you know when God commanded the rains to show the light of His clouds?
verses.37:16: Do you know the great paths of the clouds and perfect knowledge?
verses.37:17: Are your garments not warm when the earth is blown over by the south wind?
verses.37:18: Perhaps you fashioned the heavens with Him, which are most solid, as if cast of bronze.
verses.37:19: Show us what we should say to Him, for indeed we are wrapped in darkness.
verses.37:20: Who will tell Him what I speak? Even if a man speaks, he will be devoured.
verses.37:21: But now they do not see the light: suddenly the air will be thickened into clouds, and a passing wind will drive them away.
verses.37:22: From the north gold comes, and to God is fearful praise.
verses.37:23: We cannot worthily find Him; He is great in strength, and in judgment, and in righteousness, and He cannot be fully declared.
verses.37:24: Therefore men will fear Him, and all who seem to themselves to be wise will not dare to gaze upon Him."
verses.38:1: Then the Lord, answering Job from the whirlwind, said:
verses.38:2: "Who is this entangling judgments with ignorant words?
verses.38:3: Gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and answer Me.
verses.38:4: Where were you when I was laying the foundations of the earth? Declare to Me, if you have understanding.
verses.38:5: Who set its measurements, if you know? Or who stretched a line across it?
verses.38:6: On what were its bases made firm, or who lowered its cornerstone,
verses.38:7: when the morning stars praised Me together, and all the sons of God shouted with joy?
verses.38:8: Who shut in the sea with doors when it was bursting out, as though emerging from a womb,
verses.38:9: when I made a cloud its garment, and wrapped it in thick darkness as with the cloths of infancy?
verses.38:10: I surrounded it with My boundaries, and I set a bar and doors,
verses.38:11: and I said, 'This far you will come, and you will proceed no further, and here you will break your swelling waves.'
verses.38:12: Since your birth, have you commanded the daybreak and shown the dawn its place?
verses.38:13: And have you grasped the ends of the earth, shaking them, and shaken the wicked out of it?
verses.38:14: The seal will be restored like clay, and it will stand like a garment;
verses.38:15: from the wicked their light will be taken away, and the uplifted arm will be broken.
verses.38:16: Have you entered the depths of the sea, and walked about in the farthest recesses of the abyss?
verses.38:17: Have the gates of death been opened to you, and have you seen the dark doors?
verses.38:18: Have you considered the breadth of the earth? Declare everything to Me, if you know:
verses.38:19: in what way light dwells, and what the place of darkness is,
verses.38:20: so that you may lead each one to its boundaries, and understand the paths of its house.
verses.38:21: Did you know then that you were going to be born, and did you know the number of your days?
verses.38:22: Have you entered the treasuries of snow, or looked upon the treasuries of hail,
verses.38:23: which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?
verses.38:24: By what way is light scattered, and heat distributed over the earth?
verses.38:25: Who gave a course to the fiercest downpour, and a way for the resounding thunder,
verses.38:26: so that it might rain on a land without a man, in the desert where no mortal dwells;
verses.38:27: so that it might fill the trackless and desolate land, and bring forth green plants?
verses.38:28: Who is the father of rain? Or who fathered the drops of dew?
verses.38:29: From whose womb did the ice come forth? And who gave birth to the frost from heaven?
verses.38:30: Like stone, the waters are hardened, and the surface of the abyss is bound fast.
verses.38:31: Will you be strong enough to join together the glittering stars of the Pleiades, or will you be able to break up the circuit of Arcturus?
verses.38:32: Do you bring forth the morning star in its time, and make the evening star rise over the sons of the earth?
verses.38:33: Do you know the order of heaven, and will you establish its design on the earth?
verses.38:34: Will you lift up your voice in the cloud, and will a surge of waters cover you?
verses.38:35: Will you send forth lightning bolts, and will they go, and returning, say to you, 'Here we are'?
verses.38:36: Who placed wisdom in the inward parts of man? Or who gave understanding to the rooster?
verses.38:37: Who will declare the design of the heavens? And who will make the harmony of heaven sleep?
verses.38:38: When was the dust poured out on the earth, and were the clods compacted together?
verses.38:39: Will you capture prey for the lioness, and fill the appetite of her cubs,
verses.38:40: when they crouch in dens, and lie in wait in caves?
verses.38:41: Who prepares for the raven its food, when its young cry out to God, wandering about because they have no nourishment?"
verses.39:1: "Do you know the birthing time of the ibexes on the rocks, or have you observed the female deer in labor?
verses.39:2: Have you counted the months of their pregnancy, and have you known their birthing time?
verses.39:3: They crouch down for their young, and give birth, and let out groans.
verses.39:4: Their young are separated, and go off to pasture; they go out, and do not return to them.
verses.39:5: Who let the wild donkey go free, and who untied its bonds?
verses.39:6: To it I gave a house in the wilderness, and its dwellings in a land of salt.
verses.39:7: It scorns the multitude of the city; it does not hear the shout of the taskmaster.
verses.39:8: It surveys the mountains of its pasture, and searches out every green thing.
verses.39:9: Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you, or will it remain at your manger?
verses.39:10: Will you bind the rhinoceros with your strap to plow, or will it break the clods of the valleys behind you?
verses.39:11: Will you place confidence in its great strength, and leave your labors to it?
verses.39:12: Will you trust it to return the seed to you, and gather your threshing floor?
verses.39:13: The ostrich's wing resembles the wings of the heron and the hawk.
verses.39:14: When she leaves her eggs on the ground, will you perhaps warm them in the dust?
verses.39:15: She forgets that a foot may trample them, or a beast of the field may crush them.
verses.39:16: She is hardened toward her young, as though they were not hers; she has labored in vain, with no fear compelling her.
verses.39:17: For God has deprived her of wisdom, and has not given her understanding.
verses.39:18: When the time comes, she raises her wings on high; she mocks the horse and its rider.
verses.39:19: Will you provide strength to the horse, or surround its neck with neighing?
verses.39:20: Will you rouse it like locusts? The majesty of its nostrils is terror.
verses.39:21: It digs the earth with its hoof; it exults boldly; it advances to meet armed men.
verses.39:22: It scorns dread, and does not yield to the sword.
verses.39:23: Over it the quiver will resound; the spear and the shield will flash;
verses.39:24: seething and snorting, it swallows the ground, and does not heed that the blast of the trumpet is sounding.
verses.39:25: When it hears the horn, it says, 'Aha!' From afar it scents war: the exhortation of the commanders, and the shouting of the army.
verses.39:26: Is it by your wisdom that the hawk grows feathers, spreading its wings toward the south?
verses.39:27: Will the eagle rise up at your command, and set its nest on the heights?
verses.39:28: It remains on the rocks, and dwells on sheer flint crags and inaccessible cliffs.
verses.39:29: From there it watches for food, and from far off its eyes look out.
verses.39:30: Its young will lap up blood; and wherever a carcass is, immediately it is there."
verses.40:1: And the Lord continued and spoke to Job:
verses.40:2: "Does he who contends with God grow quiet so easily? Surely he who reproves God ought to answer Him."
verses.40:3: Now Job, answering the Lord, said:
verses.40:4: "I who have spoken lightly, what can I answer? I will place my hand over my mouth.
verses.40:5: I have spoken one thing that I wish I had not said, and a second, to which I will add nothing further."
verses.40:6: Now the Lord, answering Job from the whirlwind, said:
verses.40:7: "Gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and declare to Me.
verses.40:8: Will you render My judgment void, and condemn Me so that you yourself may be justified?
verses.40:9: And do you have an arm like God? And do you thunder with a similar voice?
verses.40:10: Wrap yourself in beauty, and lift yourself on high, and be glorious, and clothe yourself in stately garments.
verses.40:11: Scatter the proud in your fury, and looking upon every arrogant one, humble him.
verses.40:12: Look upon all the proud and put them to shame, and crush the wicked in their place.
verses.40:13: Conceal them together in the dust, and sink their faces into the pit.
verses.40:14: And I Myself will acknowledge that your right hand can save you.
verses.40:15: Look at Behemoth, whom I made with you; he will eat grass like an ox.
verses.40:16: His strength is in his loins, and his might is in the navel of his belly.
verses.40:17: He tightens his tail like a cedar; the sinews of his testicles are intertwined.
verses.40:18: His bones are like tubes of bronze; his cartilage is like iron plates.
verses.40:19: He himself is the beginning of the ways of God; He who made him will apply his sword.
verses.40:20: For him the mountains yield plants; all the beasts of the field will play there.
verses.40:21: Beneath the shadow he sleeps, in the hiding place of the reed and in damp places.
verses.40:22: Shadows protect his shadow; the willows of the torrent will surround him.
verses.40:23: Look, he will swallow up a river and will not be astonished, and he has confidence that the Jordan flows into his mouth.
verses.40:24: In his eyes one will capture him as with a hook, and with stakes will pierce his nostrils.
verses.40:25: Will you be able to draw Leviathan out with a hook, and bind his tongue with a rope?
verses.40:26: Will you place a ring in his nostrils, or pierce his jaw with a hoop?
verses.40:27: Will he multiply pleas to you, or speak gentle words to you?
verses.40:28: Will he strike a covenant with you, and will you take him as a perpetual servant?
verses.40:29: Will you toy with him like a bird, or bind him for your maidservants?
verses.40:30: Will friends cut him up? Will traders divide him?
verses.40:31: Will you fill dragnets with his hide, and a fish hut with his head?
verses.40:32: Place your hand on him; remember the battle, and do not speak any further."
verses.41:1: "Look, his hope will disappoint him, and with all watching he will be hurled down.
verses.41:2: Not as one who is cruel will I rouse him; for who can withstand My face?
verses.41:3: Who gave to Me beforehand, so that I should repay him? All things that are beneath heaven are Mine.
verses.41:4: I will not spare him, nor powerful words, nor those composed for supplication.
verses.41:5: Who will uncover the face of his garment? And who will enter into the middle of his mouth?
verses.41:6: Who will open the gates of his face? All around his teeth is dread.
verses.41:7: His body is like cast shields, compacted with scales pressing against each other.
verses.41:8: One is united to another, and not even a breath passes through them.
verses.41:9: One will cling to the other, and holding each other, they will by no means be separated.
verses.41:10: His sneezing is the brightness of fire, and his eyes are like the eyelids of dawn.
verses.41:11: From his mouth torches go forth, like kindled brands of fire.
verses.41:12: From his nostrils smoke goes forth, like that of a kindled and boiling pot.
verses.41:13: His breath makes coals burn, and flame issues from his mouth.
verses.41:14: In his neck strength will dwell, and destitution precedes his face.
verses.41:15: The parts of his flesh cohere to one another; He will send thunderbolts against him, and they will not be carried to a different place.
verses.41:16: His heart will be hardened like a stone, and pressed firm like a blacksmith's anvil.
verses.41:17: When he is lifted up, the angels will be afraid, and terrified, they will be purified.
verses.41:18: When a sword lays hold of him, it will not be able to stand firm, nor a spear, nor a breastplate.
verses.41:19: For he will count iron like chaff, and bronze like decayed wood.
verses.41:20: An archer will not drive him into flight; stones of a sling have been turned into stubble for him.
verses.41:21: Like stubble he will consider a hammer, and he will deride the quivering spear.
verses.41:22: Beneath him will be the rays of the sun, and he will spread out gold for himself like mud.
verses.41:23: He will cause the deep sea to boil like a pot, and will render it as when ointments bubble.
verses.41:24: Behind him a path will shine; he will consider the abyss as growing old.
verses.41:25: On earth there is no power that can be compared to him, who was made so that he would fear no one.
verses.41:26: He sees every lofty thing; he himself is king over all the sons of pride."
verses.42:1: Then Job, answering the Lord, said:
verses.42:2: "I know that You can do all things, and no thought lies hidden from You.
verses.42:3: 'Who is this who conceals counsel without knowledge?' Therefore I have spoken foolishly, and things that surpassed my knowledge beyond measure.
verses.42:4: 'Listen, and I will speak; I will question you, and answer Me.'
verses.42:5: By the hearing of the ear I have heard You, but now my eye sees You.
verses.42:6: For this reason I reproach myself, and I repent in cinders and ashes."
verses.42:7: Now after the Lord had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite, "My wrath is provoked against you and against your two friends, because you have not spoken before Me what is right, as My servant Job has.
verses.42:8: Therefore take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to My servant Job, and offer a burnt offering for yourselves; and My servant Job will pray for you. I will accept his face, so that folly may not be charged to you; for you have not spoken to Me things that are right, as My servant Job has."
verses.42:9: So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went away and did just as the Lord had spoken to them; and the Lord accepted Job's face.
verses.42:10: The Lord also turned toward Job's repentance when he prayed for his friends; and the Lord added all that had belonged to Job, twofold.
verses.42:11: Then all his brothers, all his sisters, and all who had formerly known him came to him, and ate bread with him in his house; and they shook their heads over him and comforted him over all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him; and each one gave him one sheep and one gold earring.
verses.42:12: And the Lord blessed Job's latter days more than his beginning; and he came to have fourteen thousand sheep, and six thousand camels, and a thousand yokes of oxen, and a thousand female donkeys.
verses.42:13: And he had seven sons and three daughters.
verses.42:14: And he called the name of the first, Day; and the name of the second, Cassia; and the name of the third, Horn of Antimony.
verses.42:15: Now no women were found as beautiful as the daughters of Job in the whole earth; and their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.
verses.42:16: And Job lived one hundred and forty years after these things, and saw his sons and the sons of his sons up to the fourth generation; and he died old and full of days.

notes.1:1: Vulgate simplex (lit. "simple, single-hearted, guileless") renders Hebrew tam ("blameless, complete") and corresponds to simplicitate ("sincerity") in 2:9.
notes.1:5: Vulgate benedixerint (lit. "blessed," recurring in 1:11, 2:5, and 2:9) preserves the Hebrew antiphrastic euphemism substituting "bless" for "curse" to avoid speaking a curse against God.
notes.1:11: Vulgate nisi ... benedixerit (lit. "unless he blesses") renders the Hebrew emphatic oath idiom meaning "he will certainly," with benedixerit again acting as a euphemism for "curse."
notes.1:21: The clause sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est ("just as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done") is a distinctly Vulgate reading shared with the Septuagint but absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.1:22: Vulgate labiis suis ("with his lips") appears here as well as in 2:10, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text includes the phrase only in 2:10.
notes.2:5: Vulgate alioquin ("otherwise") differs from the Hebrew adversative ("but now"), and benedicat ("bless") again preserves the euphemism for "curse."
notes.2:8: Vulgate saniem ("the discharge") explicitly specifies corrupt matter from the sore, and in sterquilinio ("on a dunghill") follows the Septuagint tradition rather than the Hebrew "among the ashes."
notes.2:9: Vulgate simplicitate ("sincerity") echoes simplex in 1:1, 1:8, and 2:3, and Benedic Deo ("Bless God") retains the antiphrastic euphemism for cursing God.
notes.3:5: Vulgate involvatur amaritudine ("be wrapped in bitterness") reflects Jerome's reading of the rare Hebrew term for blackness or gloom from the root meaning "bitter."
notes.3:6: Vulgate tenebrosus turbo ("a dark whirlwind") renders the Hebrew word for thick darkness as a dark storm.
notes.3:14: Vulgate consulibus ("consuls") renders Hebrew "counselors" using a Roman civic title, and solitudines ("desolate places") translates Hebrew "ruins."
notes.3:23: Vulgate circumdedit eum Deus tenebris ("whom God has surrounded with darkness") explicitly supplies "with darkness" where the Hebrew reads "hedged him in."
notes.3:26: Vulgate casts the verse as three rhetorical questions with Nonne ("Did I not...?")—including dissimulavi (lit. "concealed, held back")—followed by indignatio ("indignation"), whereas the Hebrew consists of declarative negative statements about lacking ease, quiet, and rest.
notes.4:5: The Vulgate supplies the explicit subject "plaga" ("a scourge" or "stroke"), whereas the Hebrew leaves the subject of "comes" and "touches" unstated.
notes.4:6: The Vulgate frames the verse as a single question listing four virtues ("Where is your fear..."), whereas the Hebrew has two equational rhetorical questions ("Is not your fear your confidence...").
notes.4:11: The Vulgate renders the poetic Hebrew term for a fierce lion ("layish") as "tigris" ("the tiger"), distinct from both the Hebrew and the Septuagint ("ant-lion").
notes.4:12: The Vulgate translates a rare Hebrew word for a faint whisper as "venas susurri ejus" ("the veins of its whisper").
notes.4:21: The Vulgate reads the Hebrew noun "yeter" in the sense of "remnant" ("those who remain") rather than "tent-cord," yielding "those who remain will be taken away from them."
notes.5:3: The Vulgate renders Hebrew "navehu" ("his dwelling") as "pulchritudini ejus" ("his beauty"), connecting it to the similar root meaning "comely" or "beautiful" (cf. 5:24).
notes.5:5: The Vulgate interprets the Hebrew term for "thorns" ("tsinnim") in the sense of shields or armed men ("armatus") and makes the fool himself the object ("ipsum"), rather than the harvest being taken from among thorns.
notes.5:6: The Vulgate renders the first clause as "Nihil in terra sine causa fit" ("Nothing on earth happens without a cause"), taking Hebrew "aven" ("affliction/iniquity") in its sense of "nothingness" rather than "affliction does not come forth from the dust."
notes.5:7: Following an ancient interpretive tradition shared with the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders the poetic Hebrew expression "sons of flame" (sparks) as "avis" ("a bird") made for flight.
notes.5:24: As in 5:3, the Vulgate renders Hebrew "naveh" ("dwelling/fold") as "speciem" ("beauty" or "appearance"), and translates the Hebrew verb "chata" in its moral sense ("you will not sin") rather than "you will miss nothing."
notes.6:2: The Vulgate reads peccata mea quibus iram merui ("my sins by which I have deserved wrath"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "my vexation" without mention of deserving wrath.
notes.6:3: In the Vulgate, feminine singular haec ("this") refers back to calamitas ("calamity"), comparing its weight on the scale to the sand of the sea, whereas the Hebrew states that it would be heavier than the sand of the seas.
notes.6:4: The Vulgate reads quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum ("whose indignation drinks up my spirit"), making the arrows' indignation the subject, whereas the Hebrew has "my spirit drinks their poison."
notes.6:6: The Vulgate renders the difficult Hebrew phrase (often translated "egg white" or "juice of the purslane") as quod gustatum affert mortem ("what, once tasted, brings death").
notes.6:19: In 6:19-20 the Vulgate uses second-person imperatives ("Examine... wait") and first-person singular ("because I hoped"; "right up to me"), whereas the Hebrew uses third-person indicatives describing the caravans looking and trusting.
notes.7:1: The Vulgate opens with the declarative statement Militia est vita hominis super terram ("Warfare [or military service] is the life of man on the earth"), whereas the Hebrew asks a rhetorical question about man's hard service.
notes.7:6: The Vulgate reads quam a texente tela succiditur ("than a web is cut off by a weaver"), whereas the Hebrew compares the swiftness of his days to a weaver's shuttle.
notes.7:9: Latin ad inferos literally means "to those below" or "to the underworld," the Vulgate's standard rendering of Hebrew Sheol (the realm of the dead), distinct from gehenna.
notes.7:15: The Vulgate reads et mortem ossa mea ("and my bones [have chosen] death"), whereas the Hebrew reads "death rather than my bones."
notes.7:20: The Vulgate renders Peccavi as a declarative statement ("I have sinned") rather than a conditional clause ("If I have sinned"), and contrarium tibi ("contrary to You") where the Hebrew has "as a target."
notes.8:5: Vulgate reads diluculo consurrexeris ("rise up at daybreak"), reflecting Jerome's literal etymological rendering of the Hebrew verb for seeking earnestly (related to the noun for dawn).
notes.8:8: Vulgate reads patrum memoriam ("the memory of the fathers"), whereas the Hebrew text speaks of what their fathers have searched out.
notes.8:14: Vulgate reads Non ei placebit vecordia sua ("His folly will not please him"), reflecting a distinct Latin reading where the Hebrew text speaks of his confidence being cut off or fragile.
notes.8:16: The Clementine Vulgate reads in ortu suo ("at its rising," from fourth-declension ortus), rather than in horto suo ("in his garden," corresponding to the Hebrew text).
notes.8:18: The Latin subject of absorbuerit ("swallows up") is unexpressed (variously understood as an indefinite agent, God, or the sun from v. 16), and Non novi te ("I do not know you") differs from Hebrew "I have not seen you."
notes.9:9: Vulgate names the constellations Arcturum et Oriona, et Hyadas ("Arcturus and Orion, and the Hyades"), where the Hebrew text names the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades.
notes.9:13: Vulgate reads qui portant orbem ("those who bear the world"), a distinctive rendering where the Hebrew text refers to "the helpers of Rahab."
notes.9:23: Vulgate frames the verse as a jussive plea about God's scourging ("If He scourges, let Him kill once for all, and let Him not laugh at the punishments of the innocent"), whereas the Hebrew text describes a sudden scourge and mockery at the despair of the innocent.
notes.9:26: Vulgate reads naves poma portantes ("ships carrying fruit"), a well-known Vulgate reading where the Hebrew text speaks of "ships of reed" (papyrus skiffs).
notes.9:35: Vulgate reads neque enim possum metuens respondere ("for I cannot answer while afraid"), a distinct reading where the Hebrew text says "for I am not so in myself."
notes.10:10: The Vulgate reads mulsisti ("milked"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "poured out."
notes.10:14: The Vulgate distinctively reads ad horam pepercisti mihi ("You spared me for an hour"), whereas the Hebrew reads "You would watch over/take note of me."
notes.10:16: The Vulgate reads propter superbiam ("because of pride") and places leaenam ("lioness") in the accusative as the quarry being captured, whereas the Hebrew depicts God hunting Job like a lion if his head lifts itself up.
notes.10:20: The Vulgate reads ut plangam paululum dolorem meum ("so that I may mourn my pain a little"), whereas the Hebrew reads "that I may have a little cheer."
notes.10:22: The Vulgate concludes with sed sempiternus horror inhabitat ("but eternal horror dwells"), whereas the Hebrew reads "and where it shines like darkness."
notes.11:6: The Vulgate reads multiplex esset lex ejus ("His law is manifold") and "far less is demanded of you by Him than your iniquity deserves," where the Hebrew speaks of sound wisdom having two sides and God forgetting part of Job's iniquity.
notes.11:7: The Vulgate renders vestigia Dei ("the footsteps of God"), whereas the Hebrew asks whether Job can discover the "depths" of God.
notes.11:12: The Vulgate reads Vir vanus in superbiam erigitur, et tamquam pullum onagri se liberum natum putat ("An empty man is raised up into pride, and thinks himself born free like the colt of a wild donkey"), differing notably from the difficult Hebrew proverb about a hollow man gaining understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a man.
notes.11:17: The Vulgate reads ad vesperam ("at evening") and cum te consumptum putaveris ("when you think yourself consumed"), and uses lucifer in its classical Latin sense of "the morning star."
notes.11:18: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew verb "dig/search" with the passive participle defossus ("buried" or "entrenched"), traditionally understood either as resting safely in the grave or sleeping secure as in an entrenched camp.
notes.12:5: A notoriously difficult verse in the Hebrew; the Vulgate construes it as Lampas contempta apud cogitationes divitum parata ad tempus statutum ("A lamp held in contempt in the thoughts of the rich is prepared for the appointed time").
notes.12:6: The Vulgate concludes cum ipse dederit omnia in manus eorum ("although He Himself has given all things into their hands"), whereas the Hebrew is commonly rendered "those who bring their god in their hand."
notes.12:17: The Vulgate reads in stultum finem ("to a foolish end") and in stuporem ("into stupor"), whereas the Hebrew speaks of counselors led away stripped or barefoot and judges made fools.
notes.12:21: The Vulgate reads eos qui oppressi fuerant relevans ("raising up those who had been oppressed"), whereas the Hebrew reads "loosens the belt of the strong."
notes.12:23: The Vulgate concludes with et subversas in integrum restituit ("and restores them completely after they have been overturned"), using the Latin legal idiom in integrum restituere ("to restore wholly"), where the Hebrew reads "enlarges nations and leads them away."
notes.13:4: Vulgate "cultores perversorum dogmatum" ("devotees of perverse doctrines") is a distinctive Latin rendering; the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "worthless physicians."
notes.13:8: The Latin idiom "faciem ejus accipitis" (literally "you accept His face," repeated in 13:10) is a biblical expression for showing partiality or favoritism.
notes.13:12: Vulgate "cervices vestræ" ("your necks") is a distinctive reading where the Hebrew refers to "your defenses" or "your mounds."
notes.13:15: Vulgate "in ipso sperabo" ("in Him I will hope") follows the Hebrew Qere tradition ("in Him") rather than the Ketiv ("not"); likewise in 13:16, Vulgate uses the personal noun "salvator" ("savior") rather than "salvation."
notes.14:4: Vulgate distinctively expands with "conceptum semine" ("conceived from unclean seed") and renders the closing clause as a question addressed to God, "nonne tu qui solus es?" ("Is it not You, who alone are?"), whereas the Hebrew reads "Not one."
notes.14:13: Vulgate "in inferno" literally means "in the lower realm" or "underworld" (traditionally rendered "hell"), denoting the abode of the dead.
notes.14:15: Vulgate "porriges dexteram" ("You will extend Your right hand") is a distinctive rendering for the Hebrew "You will long for," and in 14:16-17 Vulgate likewise reads a plea for mercy and healing ("sed parce peccatis meis ... sed curasti iniquitatem meam").
notes.14:20: Vulgate "Roborasti eum paululum" ("You made him strong for a little while") is a distinctive reading where the Hebrew reads "You overpower him forever."
notes.14:22: Vulgate includes the temporal clause "dum vivet" ("while he lives"), which has no direct equivalent in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.15:3: The Vulgate reads 'Arguis verbis eum qui non est aequalis tibi' ("You reprove with words one who is not equal to you," traditionally understood as God), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of arguing with unprofitable talk.
notes.15:11: The Vulgate asks whether it is a great thing for God to comfort Job and adds that his perverse words prevent this, differing sharply from the Hebrew ("Are the consolations of God too small for you, and a word dealt gently with you?").
notes.15:15: The Vulgate reads 'inter sanctos ejus nemo immutabilis' ("among His holy ones no one is unchangeable"), whereas the Hebrew reads that God puts no trust in His holy ones.
notes.15:30: Latin 'spiritu oris sui' uses the reflexive possessive 'sui', pointing grammatically to the ungodly man's own mouth (cf. 15:6); the Hebrew has simply "his mouth."
notes.15:31: The Vulgate reads 'Non credet, frustra errore deceptus, quod aliquo pretio redimendus sit' ("He will not believe... that he is to be redeemed at any price"), whereas the Hebrew warns him not to trust in emptiness because emptiness will be his recompense.
notes.16:5: The Vulgate reads 'roborarem vos ore meo, et moverem labia mea, quasi parcens vobis' ("I would strengthen you with my mouth, and I would move my lips as though sparing you") and has no equivalent of the Hebrew reference (v. 4) to shaking the head.
notes.16:7: The Vulgate attributes Job's distress to 'dolor meus' ("my pain") and reads 'omnes artus mei' ("all my limbs"), whereas the Hebrew speaks of God wearing Job out and desolating all his company.
notes.16:8: The Vulgate renders Hebrew 'kachashi' ("my leanness") as 'falsiloquus' ("a liar"), which serves as the grammatical subject of the hostile actions in verse 9 ('hostis meus', "my enemy") before God is introduced in verse 11.
notes.16:15: The Vulgate reads 'operui cinere carnem meam' ("covered my flesh with ashes"), whereas the Hebrew has "laid my horn in the dust."
notes.16:21: The Vulgate uses passive verbs ('judicaretur ... judicatur', "were judged ... is judged") for Job's desire for a fair hearing with God, whereas the Hebrew uses an active form ("that one might argue for a man with God").
notes.17:2: Vulgate reads "Non peccavi" ("I have not sinned"), differing markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which speaks of mockers being with Job.
notes.17:9: Latin "mundis manibus addet fortitudinem" is rendered with "mundis manibus" as a dative ("to clean hands he will add strength"), matching the Latin grammar and patristic exegesis; it can also be construed as an ablative of quality ("the one with clean hands will increase in strength"), closer to the underlying Hebrew.
notes.17:12: Vulgate reads "et rursum post tenebras spero lucem" ("and once again after darkness I hope for light"), a distinct rendering compared to the Hebrew ("light is near in the face of darkness").
notes.17:16: Latin "infernus" (also in v. 13) denotes the underworld or realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol); the Vulgate's closing question ("do you suppose that at least there I will have rest?") differs from the Hebrew, which asks whether both will go down together into the dust.
notes.18:9: Vulgate renders the Hebrew term for "snare" or "robber" as "sitis" ("thirst"), creating the distinct image of thirst blazing up against the ungodly.
notes.18:14: Vulgate reads "calcet super eum, quasi rex, interitus" ("may destruction trample over him like a king"), whereas the Hebrew refers to being marched before "the king of terrors."
notes.18:15: Latin "socii ejus qui non est" literally reads "the companions of the one who is not," reflecting the Hebrew phrase for "that which is not his" (strangers or nothingness).
notes.18:18: Vulgate uses third-person singular active verbs ("expellet", "transferet") without an explicit subject, traditionally understood as God, whereas the Hebrew has an indefinite plural ("they drive him" or passive "he is driven").
notes.19:6: Vulgate reads "flagellis suis" ("with His scourges") where the Hebrew has "His net," and "non aequo judicio" ("with no fair judgment") where the Hebrew speaks of God wronging or subverting Job.
notes.19:18: Vulgate reads "Stulti" ("Fools"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "young boys."
notes.19:20: Vulgate renders the closing clause "derelicta sunt tantummodo labia circa dentes meos" ("only the lips have been left around my teeth"), differing from the Hebrew idiom "I have escaped by the skin of my teeth."
notes.19:24: Latin "celte" ("with a chisel") is a famously rare Vulgate term (from which the archaeological word "celt" derives), corresponding to the Hebrew "forever" and perhaps arising from an early textual variant for "certe" ("surely").
notes.19:25: In vv. 25-27 the Vulgate reads in novissimo die de terra surrecturus sum ("on the last day I will rise from the earth"), rursum circumdabor pelle mea ("once more I will be encompassed with my skin") and reposita est hæc spes mea in sinu meo ("this hope of mine has been stored up in my breast"), differing markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.20:11: Vulgate-distinct reading: "the vices of his youth" (vitiis adolescentiæ ejus), whereas the Hebrew text refers to his youthful vigor.
notes.20:16: Vulgate-distinct reading: Latin Caput aspidum ("the head of asps") renders the Hebrew word rosh ("poison" or "head") literally as "head."
notes.20:23: Vulgate-distinct reading: "rain His war upon him" (pluat super illum bellum suum), understanding the Hebrew term (commonly translated as "food" or "flesh") from the root for war.
notes.20:25: The Latin opens with an abrupt participial phrase ("Drawn out... flashing in its bitterness," rendering Hebrew "gallbladder" as amaritudine) before shifting to the masculine plural substantive horribiles ("terrifying ones").
notes.20:29: Vulgate-distinct reading: "the inheritance of his words" (hæreditas verborum ejus), rendering the Hebrew term for an appointed decree from the root meaning "word."
notes.21:2: Vulgate-distinct reading: "repent" (agite pœnitentiam, literally "do penance"), taking the Hebrew root for consolation in its sense of repentance.
notes.21:10: Vulgate-distinct reading: Latin Bos eorum concepit uses bos as feminine ("cow") and translates the Hebrew clause about a bull breeding without fail as conceiving without miscarrying.
notes.21:19: The Vulgate renders the entire verse as a statement in the future tense; in the Hebrew the second clause can be read as a wish ("let Him repay him, that he may know").
notes.21:22: The Clementine Vulgate prints nominative Deus alongside nominative quispiam ("anyone"); because quispiam can only be the subject and the relative clause refers to God, the clause is translated as teaching knowledge to God (matching Deum in other Vulgate witnesses).
notes.21:33: Vulgate-distinct proper name and reading: Jerome renders Hebrew "clods of the valley" as glareis Cocyti ("the gravel of Cocytus"), naming Cocytus, the classical underworld river of wailing, and making the dead man himself ("he was sweet") the subject.
notes.22:2: The Vulgate reads comparari ("be compared"), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("be profitable").
notes.22:4: The Vulgate renders timens ("fearing") with God as the subject ("because He is afraid"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to Job's reverence ("because of your piety").
notes.22:8: The Vulgate casts this verse in the second person as a direct accusation against Job, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks in the third person of a powerful man.
notes.22:24: The Vulgate reads Dabit pro terra silicem, et pro silice torrentes aureos ("He will give flint in place of earth, and in place of flint, golden torrents"), a distinctly Vulgate promise differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's command to lay gold in the dust. Similarly, v. 25 reads contra hostes tuos ("against your enemies") rather than "your gold."
notes.22:30: The Vulgate reads Salvabitur innocens ("The innocent will be saved"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "he will deliver the one who is not innocent."
notes.23:2: The Vulgate reads manus plagae meae (literally "the hand of my blow/wound"), a distinctive rendering compared with the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("my hand is heavy") and Septuagint ("His hand").
notes.23:7: The Vulgate makes God the subject of Proponat ("Let Him set forth fairness against me"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text describes an upright man reasoning with God.
notes.23:10: The Vulgate uses the perfect tense probavit ("He has tested me like gold that passes through fire"), differing from the conditional future statement in the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold").
notes.23:12: The Vulgate reads in sinu meo ("in my bosom"), agreeing with the Septuagint against the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("more than my portion").
notes.24:1: The Vulgate frames this verse as a declarative statement rather than the rhetorical question ("Why are times not kept...") found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.24:12: The Vulgate reverses the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("yet God pays no attention to wrong"), reading et Deus inultum abire non patitur ("and God does not allow it to go unavenged").
notes.24:19: The Vulgate casts this verse as a curse on the wicked man ("Let him pass...") and renders inferos ("the underworld," the realm of the dead), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's comparison of drought and Sheol. In v. 20, the Vulgate likewise reads misericordia ("mercy") where the Hebrew has "the womb."
notes.24:21: The Vulgate renders Pavit ("has fed"), reflecting the Hebrew root for "pasture/feed" rather than the homonymous root meaning "harm/mistreat."
notes.24:23: The Vulgate reads locum poenitentiae ("a place for repentance") abused for pride, differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("gives them security"). In v. 25, the Vulgate likewise reads ante Deum ("before God") where the Hebrew has "to nothing."
notes.25:4: Vulgate-distinct phrasing: Latin explicitly renders the Hebrew preposition ("with/before God") with the participle comparatus ("compared with God").
notes.25:6: Latin literally reads quanto magis ("how much more [is this true of]"), functioning idiomatically after the preceding negative as "how much less"; Latin putredo literally means "decay/rottenness" where the Hebrew reads "maggot."
notes.26:4: Vulgate-distinct reading: where the Hebrew asks to whom words have been uttered and whose spirit came forth from the speaker, Latin asks whom Bildad wished to teach, namely, Him who made breath (eum qui fecit spiramentum).
notes.26:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders Hebrew rephaim ("shades/the departed dead") as gigantes ("giants").
notes.26:12: Vulgate-distinct rendering: Latin states that the seas were "suddenly gathered together" (repente maria congregata sunt) rather than stilled or churned up, and translates Hebrew Rahab as superbum ("the proud one").
notes.26:13: Striking Vulgate-distinct image: Latin takes the Hebrew verb in the sense of midwifery (obstetricante manu ejus, "with His hand acting as midwife") bringing forth "the twisting serpent" (coluber tortuosus), rather than piercing a fleeing serpent.
notes.26:14: Vulgate-distinct imagery: Latin reads "a small drop" (parvam stillam) where the Hebrew has "a whisper," and pairs the visual verb intueri ("gaze upon") with "the thunder of His greatness."
notes.27:8: Vulgate-distinct reading: Latin translates Hebrew chaneph ("godless") as hypocritae ("hypocrite") and frames the clause around greedily seizing (si avare rapiat) while God does not deliver his soul.
notes.27:13: The source text prints ob Omnipotente, an apparent typographical variant for the standard Clementine Vulgate ab Omnipotente ("from the Almighty"), confirmed by the ablative case of Omnipotente.
notes.27:19: Vulgate-distinct reading: Latin interprets the rich man's lying down as death leaving him empty-handed (cum dormierit, nihil secum auferet, "when he sleeps, will carry nothing away with him") and reads nihil inveniet ("will find nothing").
notes.27:20: Vulgate-distinct lexical choice: Latin reads inopia ("poverty") where the Hebrew reads "terrors."
notes.27:22: The third-person singular subject of vv. 22-23 is unexpressed in Latin, grammatically continuing the personified scorching wind/whirlwind of v. 21 (though interpreters have also understood God in v. 22 or a mocking bystander in v. 23); fugiens fugiet ("fleeing, he will flee") preserves the emphatic Latin Hebraism, and in v. 23 intuens locum ejus ("gazing upon his place") is a Vulgate-distinct reading.
notes.28:3: Latin reads Tempus posuit tenebris ("He has set a time for darkness") where the Hebrew has "puts an end/limit to darkness." The unexpressed subject of vv. 3 and 9-11 is taken here as the human miner (continuing vv. 1-2), though some traditional Vulgate commentators apply v. 3 to God.
notes.28:4: A notoriously difficult verse where the Vulgate offers a distinct reading, depicting a torrent cutting off inaccessible places forgotten by "the foot of a needy man" (pes egentis hominis, reading the Hebrew verb for "dangling" from the root for "needy").
notes.28:8: Latin filii institorum ("sons of traders/merchants") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering of Hebrew "proud beasts," paired here with the feminine leaena ("lioness").
notes.28:13: The Vulgate distinctively adds suaviter ("pleasantly") to "the land of the living," pointing to those who live in earthly ease or delight.
notes.28:16: Latin tinctis Indiae coloribus ("the dyed colors of India") is a Vulgate-distinct reading for Hebrew "gold of Ophir," taking Hebrew ketem as "dye" (as also in v. 19, tincturae mundissimae, "the purest dye") and identifying Ophir with India.
notes.29:4: Latin in diebus adolescentiae meae ("in the days of my youth") renders Hebrew "in the days of my autumn/prime," and secreto ("privately/secretly") renders Hebrew sod ("intimate friendship/counsel").
notes.29:7: The Vulgate has third-person plural parabant ("they prepared a chair for me") where the Hebrew reads first-person singular ("I prepared my seat"); similarly in v. 9 Latin specifies digitum ("a finger") rather than "hand."
notes.29:14: The Vulgate makes Job the active reflexive subject of vestivi me ("I dressed myself with my judgment as with a garment and a diadem"), whereas the Hebrew has righteousness as the subject ("it clothed me") and reads "turban" instead of "diadem."
notes.29:18: Latin sicut palma ("like a palm tree") renders Hebrew ka-chol (often read as "sand" or, via ancient tradition linked to Greek phoinix, "phoenix" or "palm tree"); in v. 19 Latin messione ("harvest") reflects the alternate meaning of Hebrew qatsir ("harvest" or "branch").
notes.30:2: Vulgate-distinct reading "et vita ipsa putabantur indigni" ("and they were considered unworthy of life itself"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text states that their vigor had perished.
notes.30:5: Vulgate-distinct reading describing the outcasts eagerly snatching wild plants from the valleys ("qui de convallibus ista rapientes..."), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text depicts them being driven out from the community with shouts as after a thief.
notes.30:11: Vulgate-distinct "Pharetram enim suam aperuit" ("For He has opened His quiver") and third-person singular "posuit" ("He has placed"), attributing the bridle as well as the affliction to God, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of loosing the bowstring and of Job's mockers casting off restraint.
notes.30:24: The Vulgate reads "non ad consumptionem eorum emittis manum tuam ... ipse salvabis" ("You do not put forth Your hand for their destruction ... You Yourself will save them"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text is obscure and is usually understood of a fallen person stretching out a hand for help.
notes.30:28: Vulgate-distinct "sine furore" ("without fury"), reflecting Jerome's reading of the Hebrew word for "sun" as "wrath" or "fury."
notes.31:2: Vulgate-distinct syntax "Quam enim partem haberet in me Deus" ("what portion would God ... have in me"), making God the subject who holds a portion in Job, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text asks what portion Job would receive from God above.
notes.31:10: Vulgate-distinct "scortum alterius" ("another's prostitute"), expressing directly what the Hebrew Masoretic Text states through the idiom of grinding for another.
notes.31:18: Vulgate-distinct "crevit mecum miseratio" ("compassion grew with me"), personifying compassion as accompanying Job from infancy and the womb, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of raising the orphan and guiding the widow.
notes.31:34: The Vulgate's "et non magis tacui, nec egressus sum ostium" ("and I have not rather kept silent, nor gone out the door") introduces a negated clause that diverges from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("so that I kept silent and did not go out the door").
notes.31:35: Vulgate-distinct "desiderium meum" ("my desire") and "ipse qui judicat" ("He Himself who judges"), pointing to God as both hearer and author of the book, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to Job's signature and an indictment written by his adversary.
notes.32:2: The Vulgate reads coram Deo ("before God"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "rather than God" (or "more than God").
notes.32:6: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew expression for holding back with the vivid Latin idiom demisso capite ("with my head bowed").
notes.32:21: The Vulgate reads et Deum homini non æquabo ("and I will not equate God with a human being"), diverging notably from the Hebrew, which speaks of not using flattering titles for any man.
notes.32:22: The Vulgate reads Nescio enim quamdiu subsistam ("For I do not know how long I will endure"), whereas the Hebrew has "For I do not know how to flatter."
notes.33:7: The Vulgate reads miraculum meum ("my wonder") and eloquentia mea ("my eloquence"), where the Hebrew has "my terror" and "my pressure" (or "hand").
notes.33:14: The Vulgate reads et secundo idipsum non repetit ("and He does not repeat the same thing a second time"), whereas the Hebrew says God speaks in one way and in two, though a person does not perceive it.
notes.33:18: Here and in verses 22, 24, and 30, the Vulgate renders Hebrew shachat ("the pit") as corruptio ("corruption").
notes.33:24: The Vulgate translates Hebrew "I have found a ransom" as inveni in quo ei propitier ("I have found that by which I may be gracious to him"). The unexpressed subject of miserebitur and dicet may be the angel of v. 23 or God.
notes.33:25: The Vulgate reads Consumpta est caro ejus a suppliciis ("His flesh has been consumed by torments"), contrasting with the Hebrew reading that his flesh becomes fresher than a child's.
notes.34:6: The Vulgate renders the opening clause 'there is falsehood in judging me' (In judicando enim me mendacium est), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'concerning my right I am considered a liar.' 'My arrow' (sagitta mea) idiomatically denotes the grievous wound inflicted on Job (cf. Job 6:4).
notes.34:14: The Vulgate distinguishes reflexive pronouns referring to God (cor suum, ad se) from non-reflexive pronouns referring to man (ad eum, illius).
notes.34:17: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew verb meaning 'bind up' or 'govern' in its medical sense as 'be healed' (sanari), rather than 'govern.'
notes.34:30: Whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads negatively ('that a godless man should not reign, nor ensnare the people'), the Vulgate reads affirmatively that God makes a hypocritical man reign because of the sins of the people.
notes.34:36: The Vulgate translates the difficult Hebrew particle as the vocative 'My Father' (Pater mi), addressing God directly, and continues with the petition 'do not leave off from the man of iniquity' (ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis), where the Hebrew reads 'because of his answers like wicked men.'
notes.35:3: In the Vulgate, Job addresses God directly ('What is upright does not please You; or what will it benefit You if I sin?'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has Job asking what advantage righteousness brings to himself.
notes.35:9: Latin calumniatorum literally means 'false accusers' or 'slanderers,' a Vulgate rendering corresponding to 'oppressions' in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.35:13: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, where both clauses are negative ('God does not hear an empty cry, nor does the Almighty regard it'), the Vulgate leaves the second clause affirmative: God does not hear in vain, and the Almighty examines the cases of each one.
notes.35:14: Latin judicare is a passive or middle imperative ('be judged' / 'submit to judgment'), rendering the Hebrew phrase 'the case is before him' as a direct command to Job.
notes.36:3: Latin 'a principio' ("from the beginning") is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew reads "from afar."
notes.36:14: Latin 'in tempestate' ("in a storm") is a distinctly Vulgate rendering; the Hebrew reads "in youth."
notes.36:19: The Vulgate construes this difficult verse as a direct imperative ('Depone magnitudinem tuam', "Lay down your greatness"), whereas the Hebrew is commonly taken as a question about whether cries or strength avail in distress.
notes.36:24: Latin 'quod ignores' ("that you do not know") is a notable Vulgate-distinct reading where the Hebrew has "to magnify."
notes.36:33: Latin 'amico suo' ("to His friend") and the clause about ascending to the light reflect a distinctly Vulgate interpretation of a notoriously obscure Hebrew verse often rendered as thunder announcing the storm.
notes.37:7: Latin 'opera sua' inside the purpose clause with subject 'singuli' most directly means "each one's own works," though traditional Vulgate commentators also note the sense "His [God's] works" (matching the Hebrew).
notes.37:9: The Vulgate retains the proper name 'Arcturus' (the northern star/constellation) where the Hebrew has 'mezarim' ("scattering winds" or north winds).
notes.37:11: Latin 'Frumentum desiderat nubes' ("Grain longs for clouds") is a distinctly Vulgate reading, interpreting Hebrew 'beri' ("moisture") as related to 'bar' ("grain").
notes.37:13: Latin 'in una tribu' ("in one tribe") renders Hebrew 'shevet' in its sense "tribe" rather than "rod [of correction]."
notes.37:23: Latin 'Digne' ("worthily") renders the Hebrew divine title 'Shaddai' ("the Almighty") by connecting it with sufficiency/worthiness; similarly in v. 22, 'formidolosa laudatio' ("fearful praise") corresponds to Hebrew "awesome majesty."
notes.38:7: The Vulgate uniquely adds "Me" and reads "praised Me" (me laudarent), whereas the Hebrew text reads "sang together."
notes.38:14: The Vulgate renders this difficult verse as "The seal will be restored like clay, and it will stand like a garment" (Restituetur ut lutum signaculum), differing from the Hebrew image of the earth changing like clay under a seal.
notes.38:31: Following Latin astronomical usage, the Vulgate names the Pleiades and Arcturus (where Hebrew has Orion), and in 38:32 similarly reads "the morning star" (luciferum) and "the evening star" (vesperum).
notes.38:36: The Vulgate specifies "in the inward parts of man" (in visceribus hominis) and renders the rare Hebrew term sekhwi as "the rooster" (gallo).
notes.38:37: The Vulgate reads "the harmony of heaven" (concentum cæli) and "make ... sleep" (dormire faciet), interpreting the Hebrew noun for "waterskins" through its homonym for a musical instrument.
notes.39:9: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew wild ox (re'em) as "the rhinoceros" (rhinoceros), a distinctive Latin reading that continues in 39:10.
notes.39:13: Whereas the Hebrew contrasts the ostrich's wing with the stork's feathers, the Vulgate states positively that the ostrich's wing resembles the wings of the heron (herodii) and the hawk.
notes.39:14: The Vulgate shifts to the second person singular ("will you perhaps warm them," tu forsitan ... calefacies ea), directly addressing Job rather than describing the ostrich warming her eggs.
notes.39:19: The Vulgate renders the rare Hebrew word ra'mah (often understood as "mane" or "thunder") as "neighing" (hinnitum).
notes.39:26: Connecting the Hebrew verb with the noun for feather or pinion, the Vulgate translates it as "grows feathers" (plumescit) rather than "soars."
notes.40:17: Latin testiculorum ejus ("of his testicles") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of Hebrew pahadaw, usually taken to mean "his thighs."
notes.40:19: The pronoun ejus in applicabit gladium ejus ("will apply his sword") is debated: grammatically non-reflexive ejus points to Behemoth's own weapon directed by his Maker, though many interpreters take it as God's sword brought near against him.
notes.40:21: Here and in v. 22 (Protegunt umbrae umbram ejus, "Shadows protect his shadow"), the Vulgate renders Hebrew tse'elim ("lotus trees") as "shadow" and "shadows."
notes.40:24: The Vulgate presents this verse as a declarative statement with an unexpressed third-person singular subject (capiet ... perforabit, rendered indefinitely as "one" and traditionally also referred to God from v. 19), whereas the Hebrew is commonly read as a rhetorical question.
notes.40:31: Latin sagenas ("dragnets") and gurgustium piscium ("a fish hut") are distinctive Vulgate renderings where the Hebrew refers to barbed irons and fish spears.
notes.41:2: The Vulgate uses a first-person verb (Non quasi crudelis suscitabo eum, "Not as one who is cruel will I rouse him"), whereas the Hebrew has a third-person statement ("No one is so fierce that he dares to stir him up").
notes.41:4: Latin Non parcam ei, et verbis potentibus, et ad deprecandum compositis ("I will not spare him, nor powerful words, nor those composed for supplication") is a distinctive Vulgate reading where the Hebrew speaks of not keeping silence concerning Leviathan's limbs, strength, and frame.
notes.41:15: The second half (mittet contra eum fulmina, et ad locum alium non ferentur) is a distinctive Vulgate reading with God as the implied subject sending thunderbolts, whereas the Hebrew describes Leviathan's flesh as cast firm and immovable.
notes.41:17: Latin angeli ("the angels") and purgabuntur ("will be purified") are distinctive Vulgate renderings of Hebrew terms commonly translated "the mighty" and "they are beside themselves."
notes.41:22: Latin radii solis ("rays of the sun") and aurum ("gold") reflect the Vulgate's distinct rendering of Hebrew terms usually translated "sharp potsherds" and "a threshing sledge."
notes.42:2: Vulgate reads "no thought lies hidden from You" (nulla te latet cogitatio), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "no purpose of Yours can be thwarted."
notes.42:4: Job here quotes God's earlier summons in 38:3, where the Vulgate has the identical wording "I will question you, and answer Me" (interrogabo te, et responde mihi). Traditional Latin commentators also read the verse directly as Job humbly asking God to listen and instruct him.
notes.42:6: Vulgate reads "I reproach myself, and I repent in cinders and ashes" (ipse me reprehendo, et ago poenitentiam in favilla et cinere), using the Latin pair for cinders and ashes where the Hebrew has "dust and ashes."
notes.42:10: Vulgate distinctively reads "turned toward Job's repentance" (conversus est ad poenitentiam Job), where the Hebrew phrase means "restored the fortunes" (or "turned the captivity").
notes.42:11: Vulgate reads "one sheep" (ovem unam), agreeing with the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text specifies a qesitah (a piece of money).
notes.42:14: Rather than transliterating the Hebrew names Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren-happuch, the Vulgate translates their meanings into Latin as Dies ("Day"), Cassia ("Cassia"), and Cornustibii ("Horn of Antimony," a vessel for eye-paint).
